transcript.text: So, if I were to create a frozen yogurt
store, this is how I would do it. So,
when I was 21, I was deciding between
this, test prep, and fitness. So, number
one, I would open my own frozen yogurt
store. And so, here are the numbers on
the top five frozen yogurt franchise in
the US. Owner pay, as you can see, after
everything, super slick. Number two,
store setup. So, most frozen yogurt
store owners charge 25 cents to 60 cents
per ounce. And yogurt costs about 8
cents per ounce, and that's pretty high
margin. Toppings cost, on the other
hand, 10 to 40 cents per ounce, which is
typically low margin. Since the average
cup size is 8 ounces, I would line the
store up from highest to lowest margin.
And so, you grab your cup, you choose
your yogurt, then you choose your hard
toppings, then you choose your fresh
toppings. So, number three, cup size. I
would only serve medium and large cups.
Because when you give someone a bigger
cup, they're more likely to fill it. If
you have a bucket like this, and then
you have to eat frozen yogurt out of it,
and the bucket's this big, you're like,
"Well, shoot, I got to kind of fill it
up a little bit, otherwise it looks
dumb." Number four, self-serve. So, most
business owners charge for small,
medium, large. But, what's actually
super smart in this industry
specifically is they charge by weight,
which the consumer is in control of.
Number five, try and become the
Chick-fil-A of the industry. So,
Yogurtland, Menchie's, Golden Spoon,
they're all almost exactly the same.
There is no Chick-fil-A in the business,
which you can do with these three
things. And so, number six, marketing.
So, I would set up close to colleges and
partner with fraternities and
sororities, and have competitions
between them to see who could get the
most yogurt, and give them some sort of
merch for the most yogurt during that
period of time. And I'd also have crazy
like 50% off types incentives to get
customer numbers in, so I could acquire
a lead that get lifetime value on for a
couple bucks.
